{{Short description|American forensic chemist}}
'''Joyce Gilchrist''' (January 11, 1948 – June 14, 2015)<ref>Ancestry.com. U.S. Public Records Index, 1950-1993, Volume 1 [database on-line]. Provo, UT: Ancestry.com Operations, Inc., 2010. Retrieved April 7, 2016.</ref> was an American [[forensic chemist]] who was accused of falsifying [[evidence (law)|evidence]] in order to help prosecutors in [[Oklahoma]]. She participated in more than 3,000 criminal cases in 21 years while working for the [[Oklahoma City Police Department]].<ref name="NYT">{{cite news |first=Jim |last=Yardley|title=Inquiry Focuses on Scientists Employed by Prosecutors |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2001/05/02/us/inquiry-focuses-on-scientist-employed-by-prosecutors.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150527151629/http://www.nytimes.com/2001/05/02/us/inquiry-focuses-on-scientist-employed-by-prosecutors.html |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |date=May 2, 2001|archive-date=May 27, 2015 |access-date=May 8, 2009|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Time Magazine" /><ref name="cacp">{{cite book|title=The Contradictions of American Capital Punishment|isbn=0-19-517820-3|url=https://archive.org/details/contradictionsof0000zimr|url-access=registration|page=[https://archive.org/details/contradictionsof0000zimr/page/161 161]|quote=Joyce Gilchrist.|access-date=May 8, 2009|author=Franklin E. Zimring|year=2003|publisher=Oxford University Press|location=New York}}</ref> Her evidence led in part to 23 people being sentenced to death, 12 of whom have been executed.<ref name="Time Magazine">{{cite magazine|first=Belinda|last=Luscombe|title=When The Evidence Lies|url=http://www.time.com/time/nation/article/0,8599,109568,00.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090428095752/http://www.time.com/time/nation/article/0,8599,109568,00.html|magazine=[[Time Magazine]]|date=May 13, 2001| archive-date=April 28, 2009|url-status=dead| access-date=May 9, 2009}}</ref> After her dismissal, Gilchrist alleged that she was fired in retaliation for reporting sexual misconduct.<ref name="nyt2" />

==Biography==
Joyce Gilchrist began working at the Oklahoma City PD  crime laboratory in 1980. Gilchrist earned the nickname "Black Magic" for her ability to match [[DNA]] evidence that other forensic examiners could not.<ref name="Time Magazine" /> She was also known for being unusually adept at testifying and persuading [[jury|juries]], thus obtaining convictions.<ref name="Time Magazine" /><ref name="fuhrman1">{{cite book|title=Death and Justice|last=Fuhrman|first=Mark|publisher=[[HarperCollins]]|isbn=0-06-073208-3|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BtY4-YryxZsC&q=Joyce+Gilchrist&pg=PA87|access-date=May 8, 2009|year=2003}}</ref> In 1994, Gilchrist was promoted to supervisor from forensic chemist after just nine years on the job,<ref name="Time Magazine" /> but her colleagues began to raise concerns about her work.<ref name="Time Magazine" /><ref name="lawar">{{cite book |last1=Dwyer|first1=Kevin|last2=Fiorillo|first2=Juré|title= True Stories of Law & Order: The Real Crimes Behind the Best Episodes of the Hit TV Show|url=https://archive.org/details/truestoriesoflaw00dwye_0|url-access=registration|page=[https://archive.org/details/truestoriesoflaw00dwye_0/page/220 220]|quote=Joyce Gilchrist.|access-date=May 8, 2009|year= 2006 |publisher= Berkley Boulevard|location= New York|isbn=0-425-21190-8}}</ref><ref name="nyt1" />

Concerns about Gilchrist's actions were first raised when a landscaper, Jeffrey Todd Pierce, who had been convicted of [[rape]] in 1986 largely based on Gilchrist's evidence despite a clean [[criminal record]] and good [[alibi]], was exonerated based on additional DNA evidence.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Innocemce Project |url=https://innocenceproject.org/cases/jeffrey-pierce/ |access-date=17 May 2026}}</ref>

Pierce, a husband and the father of two infant children, was misidentified in a police line-up. After voluntarily giving hair and blood samples to the police investigators in an attempt to clear his name, he was arrested and charged with the rape. Gilchrist claimed his hair samples were "microscopically consistent" with the hairs found at the crime scene. Pierce was cleared of the crime in 2001 after DNA evidence was re-examined, and released after 15 years in prison. Pierce subsequently filed a [[lawsuit]] against Oklahoma City, seeking $75 million and charging that Gilchrist and [[Robert H. Macy|Bob Macy]], a [[district attorney]], conspired to produce false evidence against him.<ref name="nyt2" /><ref name="cbs1" /> The suit was settled for $4 million in 2007, with one Oklahoma City councilman noting that the city could have had to pay much more.<ref name="ap1">{{cite news |title=Man gets $4 million over wrong rape conviction |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/id/wbna16792320|date=January 24, 2007|publisher=NBC News|access-date=July 19, 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201127035732/https://www.nbcnews.com/id/wbna16792320|archive-date=27 November 2020}}</ref>

==Dismissal==
Gilchrist was dismissed in September 2001 due to "flawed casework analysis" and "laboratory mismanagement".<ref name="nyt1">{{cite news |title=Police Chemist Accused of Shoddy Work Is Fired |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2001/09/26/us/police-chemist-accused-of-shoddy-work-is-fired.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151101125019/http://www.nytimes.com/2001/09/26/us/police-chemist-accused-of-shoddy-work-is-fired.html|newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |date=September 26, 2001|archive-date=November 1, 2015 |access-date=May 9, 2009|url-status=live}}</ref> An FBI investigation in 2001 concluded that Gilchrist offered testimony:“that went beyond the acceptable limits of science.”<ref>{{Cite web |title=Death Penalty Information Center |url=https://deathpenaltyinfo.org/history-of-misconduct-chronicled-in-oklahoma-county-with-41-executions |access-date=17 May 2026}}</ref> 

Robert (Bob) Macy, [[District attorney|District Attorney]] from 1980 until 2001 for [[Oklahoma County, Oklahoma|Oklahoma County]] and the State's capital, [[Oklahoma City]], has been accused of conspiring with Gilchrist on 23 of Macy's 54 death row convictions. David Autry, an Oklahoma County public defender who worked during the Macy era stated :“He would routinely withhold exculpatory evidence, he engaged in prosecutorial misconduct routinely during trials and especially during closing argument. And even when the appellate court would slap him down, he would just continue on the same course.”<ref>{{Cite web |title=Think Progress |url=https://archive.thinkprogress.org/cowboy-bob-black-magic-and-the-courtroom-of-death-78abd17d2fe1/ |access-date=17 May 2026}}</ref>

She consistently denied any wrongdoing and was never charged with any crime.

==Aftermath==
Other cases from individuals convicted on Gilchrist's testimony continue to work their way through the courts.

*Michael Blair was sentenced to death for the murder of a young girl in 1993.<ref name="nyt03" /> The evidence leading to his [[conviction]] included shafts of hair found near the girl's body and in Blair's car.<ref name="nyt03" /> New DNA evidence showed that the hair matched neither the girl, nor Blair.<ref name="nyt03">{{cite news |first=Barry |last=Scheck |author2=Neufeld, Peter |title=Junk Science, Junk Evidence |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2001/05/11/opinion/junk-science-junk-evidence.html |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |date=May 11, 2001 |access-date=May 9, 2009}}</ref>
*During the early 1990s, [[Oklahoma]] state law did not allow defense attorneys to use government funds to hire other forensic scientists to verify Gilchrist's claims. However, during appeals of Malcolm Rent Johnson's death penalty case, two forensic experts hired by the defense were critical of Gilchrist's testimony, particularly as it relied upon several "blue-colored hairs" that seemed too "ubiquitous" to be useful evidence.<ref>{{cite news |first=Jim |last=Yardley|title=Oklahoma Retraces Big Step in Capital Case |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2001/09/02/us/oklahoma-retraces-big-step-in-capital-case.html?pagewanted=2|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|pages=1–2|date=September 2, 2001 |access-date=May 9, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304123443/http://www.nytimes.com/2001/09/02/us/oklahoma-retraces-big-step-in-capital-case.html?pagewanted=2 |archive-date=March 4, 2016|url-status=live}}</ref>
*Curtis McCarty was released in 2007 after spending nearly 20 years on death row. Gilchrist initially excluded McCarty as a suspect based on microsopic hair analysis however at his trial she testified that the hairs were microscopically "in every respect" consistent with hair samples from Mc Carty.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The National Registry of Exonerations |url=https://exonerationregistry.org/cases/10645 |access-date=17 May 2026}}</ref> The courts found that Gilchrist acted to either alter or intentionally lose evidence. McCarty sued Gilchrist for her wrongdoing, but his case was thrown out on technical terms,<ref>{{Cite web|title = FindLaw's United States Tenth Circuit case and opinions.|url = https://caselaw.findlaw.com/us-10th-circuit/1576115.html|website = Findlaw|access-date = 2016-02-01}}</ref> like those of most exonerees.<ref>{{Cite web|title = Compensation for the Wrongly Convicted – The Innocence Project|url = http://www.innocenceproject.org/free-innocent/improve-the-law/compensation-for-the-wrongly-convicted|website = www.innocenceproject.org|access-date = 2016-02-01}}</ref>
*In June 2018, Johnny Edward Tallbear was released after 26 years in jail for a murder he did not commit. Gilchrist testified under oath that Tallbear's blood matched that found at the scene of the crime. DNA testing showed this to be incorrect.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Schwab |first1=Kyle |title=OKC man walks free after 1992 murder conviction vacated |url=https://newsok.com/article/5597695/okc-man-walks-free-after-1992-murder-conviction-gets-dismissed |access-date=12 June 2018 |publisher=Oklahoma City Star |date=11 June 2018}}</ref>

Over 1,700 cases in which Gilchrist's evidence was significant to conviction were reviewed by the State of Oklahoma.<ref name="nyt2">{{cite news |title=Police Chemist's Suit Says Firing Was Retaliatory |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2002/04/26/us/police-chemist-s-suit-says-firing-was-retaliatory.html |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |date= April 26, 2002|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151104175648/http://www.nytimes.com/2002/04/26/us/police-chemist-s-suit-says-firing-was-retaliatory.html|archive-date=November 4, 2015|access-date=May 9, 2009|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="cbs1">{{cite news|title=Under The Microscope|url=http://www.cbsnews.com/news/under-the-microscope-08-05-2001/|author=David Kohn|publisher=[[CBS News]]|date=July 24, 2002|access-date=May 9, 2009}}</ref> Gilchrist's attorney stated that, "The criticism of [Joyce Gilchrist] around here is second only to that of [[Timothy McVeigh]]."<ref name="Time Magazine" /> After her dismissal, Gilchrist filed a lawsuit seeking $20.1 million, claiming that her [[Termination of employment|firing]] was actually motivated by revenge, after she reported [[sexual misconduct]] by her supervisor.<ref name="nyt2" />

The [[Law & Order (season 12)|12th-season]] ''[[Law & Order]]'' episode "Myth of Fingerprints" was inspired by Gilchrist's case.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Harness |first1=Jill |title=4 Crimes That Inspired Law & Order Episodes |url=http://mentalfloss.com/article/27800/4-crimes-inspired-law-order-episodes |access-date=August 29, 2019 |work=Mental Floss |date=May 23, 2011 |language=en}}</ref>

==Death==
After her dismissal, Gilchrist relocated to [[Houston]], where she worked for a candle-making company.  She died in Texas on June 14, 2015.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://okcfox.com/archive/former-forensic-scientist-accused-of-forging-evidence-in-hundreds-of-cases-dies|title=Former forensic scientist, accused of forging evidence in hundreds of cases, dies|author=Keaton Fox|date=August 28, 2015|work=KOKH|access-date=28 March 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Disgraced Oklahoma City police chemist Joyce Gilchrist dies |url=http://newsok.com/article/5443656|date=August 31, 2015|author=Graham Lee Brewer|newspaper=The Oklahoman|access-date=October 30, 2015}}</ref>
